newsitem.title: USA: Ross expects Israeli-Palestinian accord soon.
newsitem.headline: Ross expects Israeli-Palestinian accord soon.

text.p: U.S. mediator Dennis Ross said on Wednesday that differences between Israel and the Palestinians over the West Bank town of Hebron were "clearly bridgeable" and he expected an agreement soon.

Contrary to gloomy assessments in the Middle East, Ross, who left the Israeli-Palestinian talks on Monday and returned to Washington, said the three weeks of negotiations which he chaired had made considerable progress.
"We narrowed the gaps considerably on the issues that were involved in terms of working out the mechanisms and the modalities for a Hebron redeployment," he said on MSNBC television.

"The differences that remain are clearly bridgeable and we will work to bridge those as soon as possible," he said. "In terms of reaching an agreement soon...I believe that we can do that and I believe that we will do that."

The two sides have been struggling to hammer out terms for a partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs. Israel has already redeployed in six other West Bank towns.

Ross returned to Washington after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat left the Middle East for a European tour. Israeli officials have accused him of stalling on the talks, while the Palestinians have blamed Israel for the impasse.
Lower-level negotiations are continuing in the absence of Arafat and Ross.

Ross denied that the talks had disintegrated and said that "when the leaders are available, when I've had a chance to consult with them and with the parties, there's a very good chance that I will go back in the near future."
U.S. officials said they did not expect Ross to return before the second half of next week.
The State Department meanwhile denounced what it called the "senseless killing" of an 11-year-old Palestinian boy, allegedly by a Jewish settler.

Hilmi Shousha died of a brain haemorrhage Monday. Palestinians said the security chief of a Jewish settlement adjacent to his village hit him on the head with a pistol butt but Israeli settlers said the man had not beaten him.
"We think that this was a senseless tragedy, a senseless killing, and we encourage the Israeli authorities to investigate it completely," Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
In an unusual move apparently designed to draw attention to the incident, the U.S. Consul-General in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, paid a condolence call Wednesday on the Shousha family.
"By going there, obviously we're expressing our very deep concerns about the fact that an 11-year-old boy was murdered," Burns said. "It's the kind of thing we want to stop."
